metadata.title: PISA 2009 Results: What Makes a School Successful? (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses PISA 2009 microdata covering 15-year-olds across 65 participating countries and economies, with complex two-stage sampling (schools, then students within schools). For school-principal questionnaire responses, the report states that responses are weighted to be proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in each school, indicating the use of school-level weighting when reporting principal-based indicators. For student-level reporting, the report emphasizes international comparability and participation-rate standards, and it notes that analyses account for the nested structure of students within schools within countries (e.g., via multilevel regression for within-country analyses). The manuscript does not provide explicit weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures, so the exact implementation of student sampling weights and any replicate variance estimation cannot be verified from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a descriptive policy and results report that summarizes PISA 2009 findings using correlations and multilevel regression, rather than training predictive ML models on PV-based achievement outcomes. While PISA achievement scales are typically derived using PVs in the underlying assessment framework, this volume’s provided text does not specify a PV handling strategy (e.g., Rubin’s rules) for the reported analyses. Missing-data handling is also not described in the provided excerpt beyond general notes about missing-data symbols in tables, so a specific imputation/deletion protocol for analytic models is not documented here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The target population is students aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months who have completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, regardless of institution type, full-/part-time status, or academic/vocational track. The report applies stringent technical standards for permissible exclusions, requiring overall exclusion rates within a country to be below 5% to limit distortion of national mean scores; exclusions can occur at the school level (e.g., remote/inaccessible or very small schools) or at the student level (e.g., intellectual disability or limited proficiency in the test language). The report also notes that participation-rate standards and identical administration procedures are enforced to ensure comparability across countries.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume reports PISA 2009 results focused on reading performance, with mathematics and science updated as additional domains. The assessment covered about 470,000 students (15-year-olds) across 65 participating countries and economies, using pencil-and-paper tasks in reading, mathematics and science, and in 20 countries an additional computer-based component for digital reading. Students also completed a student questionnaire (~30 minutes) covering background, learning habits, attitudes and motivation, while school principals completed a school questionnaire describing school characteristics and the learning environment; parents were surveyed in some countries via an optional questionnaire. The report emphasizes comparability through strict target-population definitions and low exclusion rates (generally <5% overall). Analyses relate performance and equity to resources, policies and practices using correlation analysis at the system level and multilevel regression models within countries, while cautioning that the results are based on non-experimental data and self-reported contextual measures.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD PISA results volume that synthesizes cross-country and within-country associations rather than training or evaluating machine-learning predictive models. Consequently, fields specific to empirical ML (e.g., main_findings rows, ML algorithms, PV-handling strategy, and missing-data imputation protocol) are not provided in the excerpted text. The report also does not specify PV combination rules or a concrete missing-data handling method for the analytic models, so those details cannot be reliably extracted from the provided content.
